claims.text: Rapid precursor reduction produces kinetically trapped, disordered FCC noble-metal HEA nanoparticles.
The metastable FCC phase has a homogeneous, random distribution of noble-metal atoms.
Random elemental mixing generates local lattice strain.
Random elemental mixing alters orbital hybridization.
Lattice strain and orbital-hybridization variations tune the adsorption energies of catalytic intermediates toward optimal values.
Optimized intermediate adsorption energies enhance catalytic performance.
Annealing above approximately 300°C provides enough atomic mobility to induce ordering and phase segregation.
Atomic ordering and phase segregation reduce the density and uniformity of optimally tuned catalytic sites.
Annealed, ordered samples will have lower catalytic activity than unannealed, disordered samples.
Annealed, ordered samples will have lower durability than unannealed, disordered samples.
The decrease in catalytic performance will correlate with atomic ordering and phase segregation observed by structural characterization.
The proposed relationship applies when synthesis kinetically traps the disordered phase and catalytic operation remains below 80°C.
Conditions permitting significant atomic diffusion can override the kinetic barriers that preserve the disordered phase.
The critical annealing temperature for pronounced ordering varies with elemental composition and synthesis conditions.
The quantitative contribution of local lattice strain to catalytic performance varies with elemental composition and synthesis conditions.

contradictions.description: The mechanism predicts loss of performance when annealing actually causes ordering or segregation, but the stated falsification rule requires both no performance loss and failure to observe ordering or segregation. Failure of the annealing treatment to alter structure is a failed mediator manipulation, not a decisive test of whether disorder drives performance. Conversely, observed ordering without a performance decrease would directly challenge the mechanism but is not covered by the stated conjunctive rule.
